claim: A fact-based memory system (Mem0) and long-context LLM inference have structurally different accuracy-cost profiles: long context wins on factual recall for most benchmarks, but the memory system becomes cheaper after roughly ten turns at 100k-token context, with the break-even point falling as context grows.
method: Compare a Mem0-based fact-extraction-and-retrieval memory system against long-context GPT-5-mini inference on accuracy and cumulative API cost, and build a cost model that incorporates prompt caching.
evidence: Three memory-centric benchmarks (LongMemEval, LoCoMo, PersonaMemv2); long-context GPT-5-mini achieves higher factual recall on LongMemEval and LoCoMo while the memory system is competitive on PersonaMemv2; under the cost model, long-context per-turn cost grows with context length even under caching while memory read cost is roughly fixed after a one-time write phase; at 100k-token context the memory system is cheaper after about ten interaction turns; no accuracy numbers given in the abstract.
not_tested: Only a single long-context model (GPT-5-mini) and a single memory framework (Mem0) are compared, so the accuracy gap may not generalize across models or memory designs; the evaluation is conversational QA rather than agentic task-solving, so it says nothing about whether retrieved facts help action selection.
title: Beyond the Context Window: A Cost-Performance Analysis of Fact-Based Memory vs. Long-Context LLMs for Persistent Agents

claim: Training LLM agents (via LoRA SFT) to use retrieved experience trajectories in-context combines the strengths of fine-tuning and training-free experience retrieval and significantly improves generalization to unseen tasks.
method: Establish a LoRA-based SFT recipe for agents, analyze design choices for experience retrieval (storage, querying, trajectory selection), and then integrate retrieved trajectories into the fine-tuning process so the agent learns to exploit them in-context.
evidence: Setting is LLM agents evaluated on unseen tasks; the SFT recipe is said to outperform several state-of-the-art agent training pipelines and the combined retrieval-plus-fine-tuning approach to significantly improve generalization; no benchmarks, models, or headline numbers are given in the abstract.
not_tested: The abstract does not say whether retrieval is compared against a random or fixed exemplar set at matched prompt length, so it is unclear how much of the gain depends on retrieval quality versus simply having trajectories in context; it also does not indicate whether the retrieval advantage holds across environments with different task-template structure.
title: Retrieval-Augmented LLM Agents: Learning to Learn from Experience

claim: Making retrieval-quality assessment an explicit action that immediately follows every search, and using the resulting scores to rescale RL advantages at the segment level, improves multi-step retrieval-augmented QA more than outcome-only rewards.
method: EvalAct enforces a coupled Search-to-Evaluate protocol in which each retrieval is followed by a structured evaluation score, and Process-Calibrated Advantage Rescaling (PCAR) rescales GRPO advantages per segment according to those scores.
evidence: Seven open-domain QA benchmarks; EvalAct achieves the best average accuracy with the largest gains on multi-hop tasks; ablations attribute the primary improvement to the explicit evaluation loop with PCAR adding consistent further gains; no numeric accuracies or model names given in the abstract.
not_tested: The setting is open-domain QA with document retrieval rather than agentic experience or exemplar retrieval, so the finding does not speak to memory banks of trajectories; the abstract reports no comparison against a retrieval-free or fixed-context baseline that would show how much retrieval itself contributes.
title: Evaluate-as-Action: Self-Evaluated Process Rewards for Retrieval-Augmented Agents

claim: A plug-and-play refiner that exploits the hierarchical structure of long documents can match the best long-context RAG baseline while using roughly 10x less computation and latency.
method: LongRefiner performs dual-level query analysis, hierarchical document structuring, and adaptive refinement, all trained via multi-task learning on a single foundation model.
evidence: Seven QA datasets; LongRefiner achieves competitive performance in various scenarios with 10x fewer computational costs and latency than the best baseline; further analysis claims scalability and efficiency; specific accuracy numbers and base models are not given in the abstract.
not_tested: The paper addresses document-level RAG for QA and does not test experience or exemplar retrieval for agents; the abstract gives no direct comparison of refinement against simply feeding the full long document to a long-context model at matched token budget.
title: Hierarchical Document Refinement for Long-context Retrieval-augmented Generation

claim: A trainable, multi-layered graph memory that distills agent trajectories into weighted, human-interpretable strategic meta-cognitions improves LLM agents' strategic reasoning and generalization and provides consistent benefits during RL training.
method: Abstract raw trajectories into structured decision paths in a state machine, distill them into high-level meta-cognitions, optimize per-meta-cognition weights by reinforcement using downstream reward feedback, and inject the optimized strategies into the agent's training loop via meta-cognitive prompting.
evidence: Agentic task-solving in complex open-ended environments; the abstract claims robust generalization, improved strategic reasoning, and consistent gains during RL training, but names no benchmarks, models, or headline numbers.
not_tested: The abstract does not compare the distilled strategy memory against a static compiled instruction set or fixed exemplars, nor against raw-trajectory retrieval at matched prompt length, so the source of the gain (distillation, weighting, or simply extra context) is unclear; run-to-run variance of the memory gain is not mentioned.
axes: compiled and static alternatives to retrieval
title: From Experience to Strategy: Empowering LLM Agents with Trainable Graph Memory

claim: AI agent workflows with dynamic multi-step reasoning improve accuracy with more compute but suffer rapidly diminishing returns, widening latency variance, and unsustainable infrastructure and energy costs.
method: A system-level characterization that measures resource usage, latency, energy, and datacenter-wide power across diverse agent designs and test-time scaling strategies, and relates design choices (few-shot prompting, reflection depth, parallel reasoning) to accuracy-cost trade-offs.
evidence: Representative LLM agents evaluated under varied test-time scaling strategies; the abstract reports diminishing accuracy returns with increased compute, widening latency variance, and high infrastructure cost, but gives no specific benchmarks, models, or numeric figures.
not_tested: The analysis covers agent compute and few-shot prompting cost but does not isolate the cost of retrieval-based experience memory versus static prefixes, nor how prompt caching changes the accounting; accuracy-cost curves are not tied to any memory or exemplar-count axis.
title: The Cost of Dynamic Reasoning: Demystifying AI Agents and Test-Time Scaling from an AI Infrastructure Perspective

claim: Under matched token budgets with long-context LMs, a simple retrieve-then-read pipeline that preserves original document order (DOS RAG) consistently matches or beats more complex multi-stage RAG pipelines, so added pipeline complexity must justify itself against this baseline.
method: Controlled QA evaluation under systematically scaled token budgets comparing multi-stage pipelines ReadAgent and RAPTOR against three baselines including DOS RAG, a retrieve-then-read method that keeps passages in original order.
evidence: Multiple long-context QA benchmarks; DOS RAG consistently matches or outperforms ReadAgent and RAPTOR; the strength is attributed to source fidelity, preserved document structure, recall prioritization within effective context windows, and simplicity; no numeric accuracies or specific models given in the abstract.
not_tested: The comparison is among RAG pipelines for document QA and does not include a no-retrieval full-document long-context arm at the same budget in the abstract's description, nor retrieval of agent experience or exemplars; the retriever is treated as given rather than compared against random or fixed passage selection.
title: Stronger Baselines for Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Long-Context Language Models

claim: A lightweight VLM that retrieves web tutorials at inference time and is trained with SFT plus self-guided rejection-sampling fine-tuning acts as a model-agnostic plug-in that consistently improves GUI agents.
method: RAG-GUI warm-starts a VLM with supervised fine-tuning, refines it with self-guided rejection sampling fine-tuning, and uses retrieved web tutorials as inference-time guidance for any VLM-based GUI agent.
evidence: Three distinct GUI tasks and two model sizes; RAG-GUI consistently outperforms baseline agents and surpasses other inference baselines by 2.6% to 13.3%.
not_tested: The abstract does not report a control in which the same tutorial guidance is compiled once into a static prompt or a fixed tutorial set is used without a retriever, so the contribution of query-time retrieval versus tutorial content is not isolated; the query used for retrieval (goal versus current screen state) is not specified.
axes: environment properties that make retrieval necessary
title: Retrieval-augmented GUI Agents with Generative Guidelines

claim: Agent self-improvement can be reframed as iterative compilation of successful trajectories into an auditable skill graph whose entries are promoted only after verifier-backed replay and contract checks, yielding reusable, verifiable capabilities rather than opaque parameter updates.
method: ASG-SI extracts candidate skills from successful trajectories, normalizes them into skills with explicit interfaces, gates promotion on verifier-backed replay and contract checks, decomposes rewards into reconstructible components for audit, and adds experience synthesis for stress testing plus continual memory control under bounded context.
evidence: A system architecture, threat model, security analysis, and a runnable reference implementation demonstrating verifier-backed reward construction, skill compilation, audit logging, and measurable improvement under continual task streams; no standard benchmarks, models, or headline numbers are given in the abstract.
not_tested: The abstract reports no comparison of the compiled skill graph against query-time retrieval of raw trajectories or against a static instruction set, so whether compilation matters beyond auditability is not established; no evaluation on standard agent benchmarks or across environments is described.
axes: compiled and static alternatives to retrieval
title: Audited Skill-Graph Self-Improvement for Agentic LLMs via Verifiable Rewards, Experience Synthesis, and Continual Memory

claim: An autoscaler that incorporates real-time prefix-cache (Radix-tree) telemetry, heterogeneity-aware tiered scheduling, and RDMA-based KV-cache preservation cuts GPU operating cost substantially under high-locality LLM traffic while meeting SLOs.
method: AdaptiveScale replaces static per-instance throughput with an Effective Token Velocity metric derived from prefix-cache telemetry, pins cost-effective GPUs to decoding while routing prefill bursts to compute-dense GPUs, and zero-copy offloads KV-cache state over RDMA during role switches; implemented on vLLM.
evidence: Evaluated with production traces from OpenAI and Azure on a vLLM-based Prefill-Decode disaggregated deployment with L40S and H100 GPUs; reduces GPU operational costs by 28% versus state-of-the-art velocity-based scalers in high-locality workloads while maintaining 99% SLO attainment.
not_tested: This is a serving-infrastructure paper: it does not measure any task accuracy or compare retrieval-based versus static-prefix prompting, so its prefix-caching gains speak only to cost of reused prefixes, not to whether static or retrieved context is preferable; results are limited to high-locality traffic patterns.
title: Context-Aware Autoscaling for Cost-Efficient Large Language Model Inference With Prefix Cache Integration

claim: A structured tool-graph experience memory that integrates planning with execution lets resource-constrained agents self-evolve from their trajectories, generalize across analogous contexts through tool reuse, and densify sparse outcome-based rewards.
method: SEARL jointly optimizes the policy and a tool-graph memory under RLVR: trajectories are abstracted into a structured memory of planning-plus-execution states, tools are reused across analogous contexts, and inter-trajectory correlations are exploited to densify the reward signal.
evidence: Evaluated on knowledge-reasoning and mathematics tasks; the abstract claims more practical and efficient learning but names no models, benchmarks or numbers.
not_tested: No comparison against directly retrieving raw interaction experiences or a static compiled tool set is stated; no ablation isolating the memory from the policy RL, and no report of memory size or per-step retrieval cost.
axes: compiled and static alternatives to retrieval
environment properties that make retrieval necessary
title: SEARL: Joint Optimization of Policy and Tool Graph Memory for Self-Evolving Agents

claim: Existing reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks and synthetic training corpora evaluate and optimize single-passage relevance in isolation, hiding retriever behaviors that matter in agentic search where the retriever must assemble a complementary evidence portfolio.
method: Build BRIGHT-Pro, an expert-annotated benchmark that expands each query with multi-aspect gold evidence and evaluates retrievers under both static and agentic search protocols; build RTriever-Synth, an aspect-decomposed synthetic corpus with complementary positives and positive-conditioned hard negatives, and LoRA fine-tune RTriever-4B from Qwen3-Embedding-4B on it.
evidence: Experiments across lexical, general-purpose and reasoning-intensive retrievers on BRIGHT-Pro under static and agentic protocols; aspect-aware and agentic evaluation are said to expose behaviors hidden by standard metrics and RTriever-4B substantially improves over its base model; no numbers are given in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether retriever gains translate into end-task answer accuracy of the search agent, and how any retriever compares to a no-retrieval or fixed-evidence baseline, is not stated.
title: Rethinking Reasoning-Intensive Retrieval: Evaluating and Advancing Retrievers in Agentic Search Systems

claim: Conditioning both retrieval and generation on a global 'mindscape' of a long document, built by hierarchical summarization, improves long-context evidence integration and sense-making over standard RAG.
method: MiA-RAG builds a mindscape through hierarchical summarization and conditions the retriever (enriched query embeddings) and the generator (reasoning over retrieved evidence within the global context) on that representation as a unified conditioning paradigm.
evidence: Evaluated on diverse long-context and bilingual benchmarks for evidence-based understanding and global sense-making; consistently surpasses baselines, with analysis showing alignment of local details with the global representation; no models or numbers are stated.
not_tested: No comparison against feeding the whole document to a long-context model without retrieval is stated, and the cost of building the hierarchical summary per document is not accounted for.
title: Mindscape-Aware Retrieval Augmented Generation for Improved Long Context Understanding

claim: Jointly optimizing SLO compliance and cost for serverless multi-tenant LLM inference can be cast as a contextual bandit over batch size, concurrency, KV-cache eviction and warm-standby choices, cutting tail latency and per-request cost.
method: A Request Profiler extracts online features (prompt length, historical KV-cache hit ratio, predicted generation length) that a contextual bandit agent uses to adaptively select batch sizes, concurrency levels, KV-cache eviction policies and warm-standby strategies.
evidence: ShareGPT and BurstGPT traces with LLaMA-2-13B and Mixtral-8x7B on NVIDIA A100 GPUs: P99 latency reduced by 38-62% versus state-of-the-art baselines, GPU utilization improved by 14-23%, per-request cost reduced by up to 27%, with a modest increase in scheduling overhead.
not_tested: This is a serving-infrastructure paper: it tests no retrieval or static-prompt policy for agents, and the effect of shared static prefixes on the KV-cache hit ratio is not isolated.
title: DeepServeCB: SLO-Aware and Cost-Aware Elastic Scheduling for Serverless Multi-Tenant LLM Inference

claim: Memory poisoning of retrieval-augmented agents can be formalized as a Stackelberg game, prior evaluation understated attack success, and a calibration-based semantic anomaly detector whose detection gradient is provably coupled to the retrieval gradient gives certified detection in continuous space, while discrete synonym substitution remains a loophole.
method: Formalize three attack classes with escalating access assumptions; correct the triggered-query evaluation protocol of Chen et al. (2024); propose MEMSAD, a calibration-based anomaly detector with a gradient coupling theorem yielding a certified detection radius, minimax sample-complexity bounds via Le Cam's method, and online regret bounds for rolling calibration.
evidence: Faithful evaluation raises ASR-R from 0.25 to 1.00 (4x); a 3x5 attack-defense matrix with bootstrap CIs, Bonferroni-corrected tests and Clopper-Pearson validation (n=1,000) shows composite defenses reach TPR=1.00 and FPR=0.00 across all attacks, while synonym substitution evades detection at delta ASR-R of about 0; no agent models or task benchmarks are named.
stated_limitations: A discrete synonym-invariance loophole marks the boundary of what continuous-space defenses can guarantee; synonym substitution evades detection, exposing a gap existing embedding-based defenses cannot close.
not_tested: No end-task utility cost of the defense (benign memories falsely rejected, task success with the defense on) is stated, and results are not tied to any specific agent environment.
title: MEMSAD: Gradient-Coupled Anomaly Detection for Memory Poisoning in Retrieval-Augmented Agents

claim: Targeted retrieval over EHR notes remains a competitive and more token-efficient alternative to long-context prompting for clinical reasoning, even as newer models handle longer inputs.
method: Define three replicable EHR tasks (imaging procedure extraction, antibiotic timeline generation, key-diagnosis identification) and, on real inpatient notes from a US academic health system, compare targeted retrieval against recent-note and long-context inputs at varying amounts of provided context across three LLMs.
evidence: GPT-5.4-mini, Mistral Medium 3 and DeepSeek V3.1: on Imaging Procedures RAG with under 8K tokens strongly beat recent-note inputs and exceeded long-context by 0.17-9.83 F1 across models; on Antibiotic Timelines under 8K retrieved tokens matched long-context recent-notes (-3.26 to +3.24 Jaccard); Diagnosis Generation was largely static across methods and models.
stated_limitations: Missing information in the clinical notes, often due to inter-hospital transfers, limited performance to some extent; diagnosis generation suggests ceiling effects imposed by documentation variability and evaluation constraints.
not_tested: Single health system and three tasks, so cross-site generality is untested; run-to-run variance and the retriever's quality against a random or fixed note selection are not reported.
title: Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation vs. Long-Context Input for Clinical Reasoning over EHRs

claim: Retrievers for agentic search should be trained on passage utility measured by both local query-passage relevance and global answer correctness, and improved iteratively together with the agent, rather than reusing similarity-based retrievers built for single-turn RAG.
method: Train the retriever with a utility signal combining local relevance and global answer correctness over multi-turn search, and alternate optimization of the search agent and the retriever so the retriever learns from the agent's evolving, higher-quality queries.
evidence: Seven single-hop and multi-hop QA benchmarks; Agentic-R consistently outperforms strong baselines across different search agents; no numbers are stated in the abstract; code released.
not_tested: No comparison of the learned retriever against a retrieval-free or fixed-context baseline, and no accounting of the extra training and per-query retrieval cost, is stated.
title: Agentic-R: Learning to Retrieve for Agentic Search

claim: Prompt optimization should accumulate a reusable, self-evolving memory of strategies and error patterns retrieved per query, rather than compile one prompt specialized to a fixed task, improving generalization across heterogeneous queries while cutting optimization cost.
method: MemAPO keeps a dual memory that distills successful trajectories into strategy templates and organizes incorrect generations into structured error patterns; for a new prompt it retrieves relevant strategies and failure patterns to compose the prompt, and updates the memory through iterative self-reflection and memory editing.
evidence: Diverse benchmarks (unnamed); MemAPO consistently outperforms representative prompt optimization baselines while substantially reducing optimization cost; no models or numbers are stated.
not_tested: Whether a single compiled prompt containing the whole strategy memory would match per-query retrieval, and the sensitivity of gains to memory size or to random retrieval, are not stated.
axes: compiled and static alternatives to retrieval
title: Generalizable Self-Evolving Memory for Automatic Prompt Optimization

claim: A map-reduce workflow over retrieved medical evidence mitigates the lost-in-the-middle problem in RAG without modifying model weights, making retrieval-augmented medical QA more robust and reliable.
method: BriefContext applies a map-reduce strategy over the retrieval results so that key information is not lost to its rank or density in the context, with no change to the LLM's weights.
evidence: Demonstrated with various LLM backbones on multiple QA datasets; no specific models, datasets or numbers are stated in the abstract.
not_tested: No comparison against simply giving the full evidence to a long-context model, and no accounting of the additional calls and tokens the map-reduce workflow costs, is stated.
title: Leveraging long context in retrieval augmented language models for medical question answering

claim: Generating task-specific context with a trained context augmentation model beats retrieving and reusing past-experience context, because retrieved context must otherwise be adapted by the execution agent at extra reasoning cost.
method: A reflection agent performs contrastive analysis over past execution trajectories to summarize useful context per task; the summaries supervise fine-tuning of a context augmentation model (CAM), which is then optimized with reinforcement learning using rewards from running the task execution agent.
evidence: AppWorld test set task completion rises from 72.62% to 81.15% and average reward on a WebShop subset from 0.68 to 0.74 versus the baseline agent; CLEAR is said to consistently outperform strong baselines; code released.
not_tested: Only two environments, with the WebShop result on a subset; the abstract does not say whether generated context is compared against a fixed compiled playbook or random exemplars, nor report the token cost of the extra CAM call.
axes: compiled and static alternatives to retrieval
title: CLEAR: Context Augmentation from Contrastive Learning of Experience via Agentic Reflection

claim: Existing memory benchmarks test passive fact retrieval, and current memory frameworks are inadequate at actively applying long-term memory to ground tool-call parameters in task execution.
method: Build Mem2ActBench with an automated pipeline that merges ToolACE, BFCL and Oasst1, resolves conflicts via consistency modeling, synthesizes 2,029 multi-turn sessions, and reverse-generates 400 memory-dependent tool-use tasks; evaluate seven memory frameworks on them.
evidence: 400 tool-use tasks derived from 2,029 synthesized sessions (about 12 user-assistant-tool turns each); human evaluation rates 91.3% as strongly memory-dependent; seven memory frameworks evaluated and found inadequate at parameter grounding (no numeric scores stated in the abstract).
not_tested: No comparison against a no-memory or full-history long-context baseline is reported in the abstract, so it is unclear how much of the deficit is retrieval versus application; the sessions and tasks are synthetic, so robustness to real interrupted user histories is untested.
axes: environment properties that make retrieval necessary
title: Mem2ActBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Long-Term Memory Utilization in Task-Oriented Autonomous Agents

claim: Search agents fail on specialized data-retrieval websites mainly because they establish the wrong site-specific retrieval state (filters, views, scopes), not because they cannot compose answers.
method: Introduce SGR-Bench, 100 expert-curated state-gated retrieval tasks across six source families and 12 public data ecosystems, with paired constraint-guided and goal-oriented formulations, and evaluate agents plus manually audit failed trajectories.
evidence: Eight CLI-based agentic LLM systems and three commercial search-agent products; best system reaches 66.18% item-level F1 with much lower row-level F1; audit of 156 failed CLI trajectories attributes 37.2% to retrieval-scope drift, 27.6% to criterion mismatch, and 10.3% to final answer composition.
not_tested: Whether providing agents with stored site-specific procedures (e.g., a playbook of how to configure each site) or prior successful trajectories would fix scope drift is not tested; run-to-run variance of the agents is not reported in the abstract.
axes: environment properties that make retrieval necessary
title: SGR-Bench: Benchmarking Search Agents on State-Gated Retrieval

claim: For agentic search, letting the agent interact with the raw corpus directly through general-purpose terminal tools outperforms fixed top-k lexical, dense and reranking retrievers, because retrieval quality depends on the resolution of the corpus interface, not only on reasoning.
method: Direct corpus interaction (DCI): an agent searches the raw corpus with grep, file reads, shell commands and lightweight scripts, with no embedding model, vector index or retrieval API, and is evaluated against conventional retrievers.
evidence: IR benchmarks and end-to-end agentic search tasks; substantially outperforms strong sparse, dense and reranking baselines on several BRIGHT and BEIR datasets; strong accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus and multi-hop QA without any conventional semantic retriever (no specific numbers stated in the abstract).
not_tested: Token and latency cost of multi-step terminal search versus a single top-k call is not quantified in the abstract; the approach is not tested on corpora too large for grep-style scanning, and the dependence of gains on agent strength is asserted rather than measured across model sizes.
title: Beyond Semantic Similarity: Rethinking Retrieval for Agentic Search via Direct Corpus Interaction

claim: Retrieval-augmented few-shot prompting with semantically similar examples consistently beats random-example few-shot prompting, zero-shot prompting and fine-tuned Gemini on code vulnerability detection, though a fine-tuned CodeBERT still scores higher.
method: Systematic comparison with Gemini-1.5-Flash of random few-shot prompting, retrieval-augmented prompting with semantically similar examples, and retrieval-based labeling without model inference, plus zero-shot and fine-tuned baselines (Gemini-1.5-Flash, DistilBERT, DistilGPT2, CodeBERT).
evidence: Code vulnerability detection over a predefined set of vulnerability categories; retrieval-augmented prompting at 20 shots reaches F1 74.05% and partial match accuracy 83.90%, versus zero-shot F1 36.35% / 20.30% and fine-tuned Gemini F1 59.31% / 53.10%; fine-tuned CodeBERT reaches F1 91.22% / 91.30%.
not_tested: Only one prompting model (Gemini-1.5-Flash) and one task, so generality of the retrieval advantage is untested; a fixed curated exemplar set and shot counts beyond 20 (saturation or a whole-bank long-context prompt) are not reported in the abstract.
axes: compiled and static alternatives to retrieval
title: Retrieval-Augmented Few-Shot Prompting Versus Fine-Tuning for Code Vulnerability Detection

claim: Correctly selected summarized experience from related tasks improves programming-agent resolution accuracy and substantially reduces runtime and token cost, while unfiltered or incorrectly selected experience gives limited or negative benefit.
method: SWE-ContextBench augments 300 SWE-Bench Lite tasks with 99 related tasks derived from real GitHub issue and pull-request dependency and reference relationships, forming task sequences, and evaluates experience reuse under oracle-guided and autonomous retrieval with full trajectories or compact summaries.
evidence: 300 base plus 99 related tasks from SWE-Bench Lite; metrics are prediction accuracy, time efficiency and cost efficiency; correctly selected summarized experience improves accuracy and cuts runtime and token cost, especially on harder tasks, whereas unfiltered or wrongly selected experience helps little or hurts (no numbers stated in the abstract).
not_tested: The abstract does not state which agents or models were evaluated or the run-to-run variance of the gains; the related tasks are drawn from explicit dependency links, so gains on unrelated or diverse task sequences are not measured.
axes: environment properties that make retrieval necessary
title: SWE Context Bench: A Benchmark for Context Learning in Coding

claim: The load-bearing memory for long-running coding agents is situationally cued operational facts that must be delivered deterministically by the harness, because agents almost never voluntarily read or write document-style memory.
method: A two-tier design theory grounded in cognitive literature, a cue-anchored memory model with first-class trigger conditions (path, symbol, semantic, event, temporal) evaluated deterministically by the harness, and a controlled evaluation on a real coding task plus a repeated-compaction decay probe.
evidence: On a real coding task, voluntary memory use was 0 operations in 114 turns even with a pre-seeded store; deterministic injection delivered in every seeded run with zero false alarms; 39% of intra-session re-reads re-bought content paid for before a compaction boundary; ten conversation-only facts vanished at the first summary and were absent from 106 of 108 compactions, while harness-injected facts arrived intact through all 138 compact-resumes.
not_tested: The evaluation is a single coding task with a small set of seeded facts, so cross-task generality and effect on task success rate are not shown; the model does not measure whether cue-triggered injection adds noise or cost when the memory store grows large.
axes: compiled and static alternatives to retrieval
title: Delivery, Not Storage: Cue-Anchored Working Memory as a Harness Property for Coding Agents

claim: Memory systems should be evaluated on whether they internalize environment-specific experience, and a coding agent that gathers evidence from stored trajectories substantially outperforms RAG-based memory on this, at a high latency cost.
method: LongMemEval-V2: 451 curated questions covering static state recall, dynamic state tracking, workflow knowledge, environment gotchas and premise awareness, paired with history trajectories, in a context-gathering formulation; two proposed memory methods, AgentRunbook-R (RAG with pools of state observations, events and strategy notes) and AgentRunbook-C (trajectories as files searched by a coding agent in a sandbox).
evidence: Web-agent environments with histories of up to 500 trajectories and 115M tokens; AgentRunbook-C reaches 72.5% average accuracy versus 48.5% for the strongest RAG baseline and 69.3% for an off-the-shelf coding agent baseline; coding-agent methods have high latency.
stated_limitations: Despite the strong performance gains, coding agent based methods have high latency costs; substantial room for improvement remains.
not_tested: The benchmark scores evidence gathering for question answering rather than downstream task success, so whether recalled experience improves action-taking is not shown; a whole-history long-context baseline is not mentioned, and token cost is only characterized as latency.
axes: environment properties that make retrieval necessary
title: LongMemEval-V2: Evaluating Long-Term Agent Memory Toward Experienced Colleagues

claim: A separate RL-trained proxy model that uses knowledge-graph reasoning to decide when and how to retrieve can control adaptive RAG without fine-tuning the LLM and generalizes across retrievers and LLMs.
method: SPARKLE: a plug-and-play proxy retrieval policy, independent of the retriever and the LLM, optimised with reinforcement learning treating retriever and LLM as environment, with a binary tree-structured rollout strategy for exploration.
evidence: Three in-domain and four out-of-domain QA benchmarks; average improvements over state-of-the-art baselines of 9.17% in-domain and 2.85% out-of-domain (specific models and retrievers not named in the abstract).
not_tested: Cost of the additional proxy model and knowledge-graph reasoning per query is not reported in the abstract; the policy is evaluated on QA, not on agentic tasks where the query is a goal or state, and the value of retrieval decisions versus always-retrieve is not quantified.
title: SPARKLE: A Structured and Plug-and-play Agentic Retrieval Policy for Adaptive RAG Models

claim: Treating knowledge-graph context construction as a budgeted sequential decision process yields higher multi-hop QA accuracy with smaller, provenance-preserving contexts and lower, more predictable latency than static k-hop expansion or GraphRAG.
method: CLAUSE, a three-agent neuro-symbolic framework (Subgraph Architect, Path Navigator, Context Curator) coordinated by Lagrangian-Constrained Multi-Agent PPO, with per-query budgets on edge edits, interaction steps and selected tokens.
evidence: HotpotQA, MetaQA and FactKG; higher EM@1 with reduced subgraph growth and end-to-end latency at equal or lower token budgets; on MetaQA-2-hop, +39.3 EM@1 over GraphRAG with 18.6% lower latency and 40.9% lower edge growth.
not_tested: Training cost of LC-MAPPO and transfer of the learned policies to new knowledge graphs are not described in the abstract; the comparison excludes a long-context baseline that simply includes a large static subgraph, and variance across runs is not reported.
title: CLAUSE: Agentic Neuro-Symbolic Knowledge Graph Reasoning via Dynamic Learnable Context Engineering

claim: LLM-based data augmentation improves compact dual-encoder retrieval, but the benefit saturates beyond a certain augmentation scale even with diverse strategies, smaller augmentation LLMs are competitive with larger ones, and the gain is largest for poorly pre-trained retrievers.
method: A study of over 100 experimental settings varying retrieval models, augmentation models and augmentation strategies, including out-of-distribution evaluation and analysis by retriever pre-training level.
evidence: Compact dual-encoder retrievers with LLM-generated augmentation across more than 100 settings; augmentation helps but diminishes past a scale threshold; smaller LLM augmenters match larger ones; benefit is greatest for models that are not well pre-trained (no specific numbers or benchmark names stated in the abstract).
not_tested: The study concerns training-data augmentation for retrievers, not retrieval at inference time for agents, so nothing is shown about how retrieved items affect downstream LLM task performance; the abstract does not name the OOD benchmarks or quantify the saturation point.
title:
Evaluating the Effectiveness and Scalability of LLM-Based Data
  Augmentation for Retrieval

claim: Long-term memory and state tracking in dynamic, multi-platform enterprise agent environments is largely unsolved: the best model (GPT-5) reaches only 60% Correctness on MEMTRACK, with failures in long-horizon memory use, cross-platform dependencies and contradiction resolution.
method: Build a benchmark of chronologically interleaved timelines across Slack, Linear and Git with noisy, conflicting, cross-referring events plus codebase/file-system exploration, curated via manual expert design and agent-based synthesis, and score memory-augmented agents on Correctness, Efficiency and Redundancy.
evidence: Experiments across SoTA LLMs and several memory backends on MEMTRACK; best-performing GPT-5 achieves 60% Correctness; no other numbers stated.
not_tested: Does not compare query-time retrieval against a static compiled summary of the timeline or against placing the whole timeline in a long context; does not report run-to-run variance of memory-backend gains or token cost per backend.
axes: environment properties that make retrieval necessary
title:
MEMTRACK: Evaluating Long-Term Memory and State Tracking in
  Multi-Platform Dynamic Agent Environments

claim: Retrievers for agentic search should be trained from agent interaction trajectories rather than human click logs, and doing so improves evidence recall, task success and execution efficiency across agent architectures and scales.
method: Analyze search-agent trajectories to identify utility signals (browsing actions, unbrowsed rejections, post-browse reasoning traces), then LRAT mines retrieval supervision from these and trains retrievers with relevance-intensity-weighted optimization.
evidence: In-domain and out-of-domain deep research benchmarks across diverse agent architectures and scales; retrievers trained with LRAT consistently improve evidence recall, end-to-end task success and execution efficiency; no headline numbers stated.
not_tested: Does not compare the learned retriever against random or fixed exemplar/document sets to show the retriever is not decorative; does not test whether gains transfer to experience/trajectory memory banks rather than document corpora, or quantify token cost.
title: Learning to Retrieve from Agent Trajectories

claim: Retrieval quality is the main determinant of end-to-end RAG quality in knowledge-management QA, and 256-token chunking with overlap, top-1 retrieval and grounded prompting are robust design choices, while abstention-oriented prompting is a separate operating point rather than a default.
method: Component-level benchmark combining embedding and generation models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B-It) with retrieval measured by recall, latency and storage and generation by ROUGE-L, EM, token-F1, BERTScore, semantic similarity, answer relevance and faithfulness, plus SQuAD/HotpotQA, grounded and abstention prompting, error analysis and long-context stress testing.
evidence: Best retrieval setup all-mpnet-base-v2, 256-token chunks, 64-token overlap, top-1: Recall@1 = 0.938; Gemma-2-9B-It best grounded-abstain configuration ROUGE-L 0.631, EM 0.456, token-F1 0.631, BERTScore F1 0.767; Llama-3-8B best faithfulness 0.241; HNSW matched exact-search quality with lower latency.
stated_limitations: The design narrows practical claims to what is supported by multi-dataset evidence, error analysis and long-context testing.
not_tested: Does not test a no-retrieval or fixed-context baseline against retrieval on the same generators; does not report run-to-run variance or prompt caching/token accounting for the long-context stress condition.
title: Comparative evaluation of embedding and generative model combinations in retrieval-augmented generation pipelines

claim: An agentic long-context RAG pipeline that combines chunk retrieval with cached ground-truth MCQs and a one-million-token context yields the most accurate context-specific quiz generation for engineering education.
method: Modular agent pipeline (parsing, chunking/storage, embedding/indexing, verification, retriever with cosine similarity and multilingual re-ranking, selector, response agent using cached ground-truth MCQs, evaluator) built on Gemini 1.5's 1M-token window, compared against raw, chunk-only and chunks+cache configurations.
evidence: 150-question MCQ benchmark: Gemini accuracy 78.00% (raw), 84.00% (chunks), 89.33% (chunks+cache), 93.33% (1M context+cache); GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 3.7 show complementary strengths in precision and confidence.
not_tested: Does not isolate a 1M-context-without-cache or cache-without-retrieval condition, so the retriever's contribution beyond the cached exemplars and long context is unclear; does not report token cost or run-to-run variance on the 150-question set.
axes: compiled and static alternatives to retrieval
title: Agentic AI Quiz-Based Learning System: Enhancing MCQ Generation via Long-Context Cached Retrieval-Augmented Generation

claim: Agent memory should be evaluated as test-time evolution over sequential task streams rather than static conversational recall, and the proposed ReMem action-think-memory pipeline enables continual improvement over an ExpRAG experience-retrieval baseline.
method: Structure datasets into sequential task streams requiring agents to search, adapt and update memory after each interaction; unify and implement over ten memory modules and compare them, plus the ExpRAG retrieval baseline and the ReMem refine pipeline.
evidence: Over ten memory modules evaluated across 10 multi-turn goal-oriented and single-turn reasoning/QA datasets; no headline numbers stated.
not_tested: Does not compare experience retrieval against a fixed exemplar set or compiled instructions built once from the stream; does not report run-to-run noise of memory gains or how much of the gain comes from near-duplicate tasks within a stream.
axes: environment properties that make retrieval necessary
title: Evo-Memory: Benchmarking LLM Agent Test-time Learning with Self-Evolving Memory

claim: In-context learning in unified multimodal models is non-monotonic and task-dependent, and a capability-oriented taxonomy plus a lightweight Context-Adaptive Prototype Modulator stabilizes few-shot adaptation and outperforms larger multimodal baselines on most understanding ICL tasks.
method: Define a six-level taxonomy of demonstration roles, build the UniICL-760K corpus of curated 8-shot episodes over 15 subtasks and UniICL-Bench, and add a plug-and-play prototype-modulator module.
evidence: UniICL-Bench evaluation; approach outperforms larger-parameter multimodal LLM baselines on most understanding ICL tasks; no numbers stated.
not_tested: Does not test retrieved versus fixed or random demonstration sets, nor scaling beyond 8 shots to assess saturation with the number of exemplars.
title: UniICL: Systematizing Unified Multimodal In-context Learning through a Capability-Oriented Taxonomy

claim: Existing memory benchmarks decouple memorization from action, and agents that near-saturate long-context memory benchmarks like LoCoMo perform poorly when memory must be acquired through interaction and used to guide later interdependent subtasks.
method: Introduce MemoryArena, a gym of human-crafted multi-session tasks with explicitly interdependent subtasks across web navigation, preference-constrained planning, progressive information search and sequential formal reasoning, in which agents distill experiences into memory and reuse it.
evidence: Agents evaluated across the four task families; agents near-saturated on LoCoMo perform poorly in MemoryArena; no headline numbers stated.
not_tested: Does not compare retrieval-based memory against a static compiled summary or full long-context replay of earlier sessions; does not report run-to-run noise or token cost of memory mechanisms.
axes: environment properties that make retrieval necessary
title: MemoryArena: Benchmarking Agent Memory in Interdependent Multi-Session Agentic Tasks

claim: Attention scores of selected retrieval heads can be trained into a lightweight listwise reranker that outperforms state-of-the-art pointwise and listwise rerankers and sets a new state of the art on LoCoMo.
method: Train small models (e.g. 4B) to estimate passage-query relevance from attention scores of selected heads over the entire candidate shortlist, yielding continuous relevance scores that allow training on arbitrary retrieval datasets; extensions include contextual augmentation of candidates and using middle-layer heads.
evidence: Outperforms existing pointwise and listwise rerankers on Wikipedia and long narrative datasets and achieves state of the art on LoCoMo with a 4B-scale model; no numbers stated.
not_tested: Does not compare the reranker against feeding the full long context without reranking or against random/fixed passage selection; does not report end-to-end token cost or run-to-run variance.
title: Query-focused and Memory-aware Reranker for Long Context Processing

claim: Retrieval objectives should shift from topical relevance to LLM-centric utility, because in RAG retrieval effectiveness must be judged by its contribution to generation quality rather than relevance-ranking metrics alone.
method: A tutorial presenting a unified framework of LLM-agnostic versus LLM-specific utility, context-independent versus context-dependent utility, and connections to LLM information needs and agentic RAG, synthesized from recent advances.
evidence: Conceptual synthesis; no experiments, models or benchmark numbers stated.
not_tested: Provides no empirical comparison of utility-trained retrievers against relevance-trained, random or fixed-context baselines; does not quantify when retrieval is unnecessary given a long context.
title: Beyond Relevance: Utility-Centric Retrieval in the LLM Era

claim: No single agent-memory architecture dominates across workloads; effectiveness depends on aligning memory structure with the workload bottleneck, and localized maintenance is more cost-efficient than global reorganization.
method: Decompose agent memory into four modules (representation and storage, extraction, retrieval and routing, maintenance) and evaluate 12 memory systems and two reference baselines across five benchmark workloads spanning 11 datasets, with fine-grained ablations and cost-performance analysis.
evidence: 12 memory systems and two reference baselines on five workloads over 11 datasets; ablations quantify representation fidelity, retrieval precision, update correctness and long-horizon stability; localized maintenance is more cost-efficient than global reorganization; no headline numbers stated.
not_tested: Does not report whether the two reference baselines include a static compiled context or full long-context replay, nor run-to-run noise of the reported differences; cross-environment generality beyond the five workloads is not addressed.
axes: environment properties that make retrieval necessary
title: Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System?

claim: A multi-agent RAG framework with a GMM-based hybrid multi-modal retrieval strategy and an iterative exploration-summarization-reflection agent workflow substantially improves retrieval-augmented reasoning over visually rich documents.
method: Introduce the ViDoSeek dataset for RAG over visually rich documents requiring complex reasoning, then propose ViDoRAG, which combines GMM-based hybrid (textual plus visual) retrieval with an iterative multi-agent workflow of exploration, summarization and reflection that scales reasoning tokens at test time.
evidence: Experiments on the new ViDoSeek benchmark; ViDoRAG outperforms existing methods by over 10% on ViDoSeek; specific reader models and absolute scores not stated in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether the >10% gain comes from the hybrid retrieval versus the extra reasoning tokens of the agent workflow is not separated in the abstract; no evaluation on benchmarks other than the authors' own ViDoSeek, and no token/latency cost accounting for the iterative agent loop is reported.
title: ViDoRAG: Visual Document Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Dynamic Iterative Reasoning Agents

claim: Decomposed uncertainty signals estimated from LLM hidden states in a single forward pass can decide transparently when to trigger retrieval (knowledge insufficiency) versus when to apply extra reasoning (ambiguity or conflict) in QA.
method: Estimate two distinct uncertainty signals, knowledge insufficiency and knowledge ambiguity/conflict, from the LLM's internal representations in one forward pass, and use them as an adaptive policy that triggers RAG on insufficiency and additional reasoning on high ambiguity/conflict.
evidence: Setting is question answering with adaptive retrieval and reasoning; no specific models, benchmarks or headline numbers are stated in the abstract.
not_tested: No quantitative comparison against always-retrieve, never-retrieve or multi-step prompting baselines is reported in the abstract; the approach requires hidden-state access, so applicability to closed API models and to agentic (non-QA) tasks is untested.
title: Interpretable Uncertainty for Adaptive Retrieval and Reasoning in Question Answering

claim: Because agent memory is a bounded, highly correlated and often duplicated dialogue stream rather than a heterogeneous corpus, fixed top-k similarity retrieval returns redundant context, and retrieval should instead operate over a hierarchy of decoupled semantic components with expansion to raw episodes only when it reduces reader uncertainty.
method: xMemory disentangles memories into semantic components organised into a hierarchy of intact units via a sparsity-semantics objective that guides memory split and merge, then retrieves top-down by selecting a compact diverse set of themes and semantics and expanding to episodes and raw messages only when that reduces the reader's uncertainty.
evidence: Experiments on LoCoMo and PerLTQA across three recent LLMs (unnamed in the abstract) show consistent gains in answer quality and token efficiency; no specific numbers stated.
not_tested: Only long-conversation QA benchmarks are used, so whether the decoupling-aggregation advantage transfers to agentic task environments is untested; the abstract does not compare against a long-context baseline that simply includes the whole dialogue stream, nor report construction cost of the hierarchy.
axes: environment properties that make retrieval necessary
title: Beyond RAG for Agent Memory: Retrieval by Decoupling and Aggregation

claim: Across a controlled corpus-size sweep, no RAG paradigm wins unconditionally: an agentic file-system search leads at small corpora, but BM25 lexical retrieval overtakes it around 10 million corpus tokens and leads at every larger tier, making global candidate ranking the strongest scalable default with agentic reasoning best applied after ranked discovery.
method: Vary corpus size along 28 strictly nested tiers spanning roughly 450-fold while holding questions and a fixed bedrock of relevant and adversarial documents unchanged, and compare lexical, dense, graph-based and agentic RAG under one reader model and one judging protocol, measuring accuracy, construction and query tokens, and latency.
evidence: Single reader model and judging protocol; File-System Agent leads at the smallest shared tiers but costs 39 times more query tokens at the bedrock; BM25 overtakes around 10M corpus tokens with a margin approaching 20 points at full scale and anchors the low-cost Pareto frontier; dense retrieval is efficient but less accurate; graph-based RAG hits construction walls and its scalable variants stay below BM25.
not_tested: Only one reader model and one question set are used, so whether the crossover point shifts with reader capability or task type is untested; the study covers document corpora, not experience or trajectory banks, so the scaling conclusions for agent memory are not established.
title: BM25 Wins at Scale: A Scaling Study of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Paradigms

claim: In-context routing over a capability registry collapses as the registry grows, whereas an offline-enriched retrieve-then-rank pipeline degrades gracefully and is both more accurate and far cheaper at scale.
method: Recast capability discovery as search: an offline enrichment step turns sparse MATS component metadata into searchable profiles, and an online retrieve-then-rank pipeline returns a ranked shortlist without invoking candidates, compared against Full-Ctx (whole registry in the prompt) and Search&Pick (LLM with a search tool) baselines using one fixed configuration across agent, tool and skill registries.
evidence: From N=10 to 7,278 capabilities, in-context routing Match@1 falls 0.85 to 0.12 while retrieve-then-rank falls 0.81 to 0.39; the reranker ranks the right capability first 0.70-0.87 of the time once retrieval finds it; crossover around N=500 in the Nova Micro sweep; at full scale the pipeline leads Search&Pick by 6.5 pp at about half the cost and cuts cost 70x versus Full-Ctx; deployed in production on a large multi-agent platform.
not_tested: Match@1 measures whether the right capability is selected, not end-task success after invoking it; the retrieve-then-rank pipeline's own accuracy still falls to 0.39 at full scale, and the abstract does not report how much of that is retrieval recall failure versus reranking error or how the sweep behaves with stronger routing LLMs than Nova Micro.
title: Enrich-Retrieve-Rank: Scaling Capability Discovery Beyond In-Context Routing

claim: In memory-augmented LLM agents, the retrieval method dominates performance far more than the write strategy, raw chunked storage matches or beats expensive lossy write pipelines, and failures manifest mostly at the retrieval stage rather than at utilization.
method: A diagnostic framework applied to a 3x3 study crossing three write strategies (raw chunks, Mem0-style fact extraction, MemGPT-style summarization) with three retrieval methods (cosine, BM25, hybrid reranking), plus failure analysis separating retrieval-stage from utilization-stage breakdowns.
evidence: On LoCoMo, average accuracy spans 20 points across retrieval methods (57.1% to 77.2%) but only 3-8 points across write strategies; raw chunked storage with zero LLM calls matches or outperforms fact extraction and summarization; failure analysis attributes most breakdowns to retrieval rather than utilization.
not_tested: Only the LoCoMo conversational QA benchmark is used, so whether retrieval dominance holds for procedural or task-oriented agent memory is untested; the abstract reports no run-to-run variance and no comparison against putting the full history in a long context without retrieval.
title: Diagnosing Retrieval vs. Utilization Bottlenecks in LLM Agent Memory

claim: Current LLM agents rarely distill episodic experience into robust reusable procedural skills: raw-trajectory reuse frequently outperforms distilled skills, skill gains are unstable under frozen deployment, and writing more skills or larger resource libraries adds coverage but also episode-specific drift and procedural clutter.
method: SkillEvolBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 180 tasks across six real-world agent environments organised into role-conditioned task families with shared latent procedures; agents learn from acquisition tasks, update an external skill library from compacted trajectories and verifier feedback, then face frozen deployment tasks testing context shift, adversarial shortcuts and composition, with self-generated and curated-start skill evolution compared against no-skill and raw-trajectory controls.
evidence: Ten model configurations and three agent harnesses on 180 tasks in six environments; agents adapt locally but rarely form robust reusable skills, raw-trajectory reuse frequently beats distilled skills, skill-based gains on specific deployment axes are unstable under frozen deployment, and capacity/cost analyses show larger Tier-3 libraries are not sufficient; no headline numbers stated in the abstract.
not_tested: The abstract does not say how raw trajectories are selected for reuse (retrieved versus fixed), so the retriever's contribution to the raw-trajectory advantage is unclear; it also does not report run-to-run noise of the skill-condition gains that it calls unstable, or a long-context condition that supplies all trajectories at once.
axes: compiled and static alternatives to retrieval
environment properties that make retrieval necessary
title: SkillEvolBench: Benchmarking the Evolution from Episodic Experience to Procedural Skills

claim: In multi-hop agentic RAG, post-hoc trace-based diagnosis loses the signal needed to identify an injected retrieval fault once the downstream trajectory changes, so propagation depth must be an explicit evaluation axis for failure attribution.
method: AgenticRAG-FP, an interventional benchmark that injects a certified fault at a specified hop, re-executes the downstream trajectory, and scores diagnosers against the known intervention, comparing coverage-based diagnosis with a frozen-hop counterfactual probe and a smaller content-corruption study.
evidence: Strict dense Claude Haiku 4.5 sweep on 80 three-hop MuSiQue questions: coverage-based diagnosis is 0.91 at hop 1 and 0.00 at hops 2 and 3 (n=43, 36, 21 failed trajectories); in the content-corruption study at depth 2 (18 failed cases) coverage-based diagnosis is 0.00 and the frozen-hop counterfactual probe is 0.67 in an exploratory pooled comparison; depth-3 content estimates are descriptive only (three failed cases).
stated_limitations: Depth-3 content estimates are descriptive only because they contain three failed cases; the depth-2 counterfactual comparison is an exploratory pooled comparison distinguished from broad evidence of post-hoc signal loss as a small-sample method comparison.
not_tested: Only one agent model (Claude Haiku 4.5) and one dataset (80 MuSiQue questions) are used, so generality across models and retrieval settings is untested; the benchmark evaluates fault attribution, not whether the agent's later retrieval actually repairs trajectories at a measurable rate.
title: When Failures Propagate: Causal Failure Attribution in Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation

claim: An agent can build useful procedural memory before seeing any target-environment tasks by practising on proposer-controlled synthetic tasks with validated trajectory insertion, reaching performance competitive with playbook methods built from real offline or online experience at lower deployment cost.
method: Preping: a Proposer generates synthetic tasks conditioned on a structured proposer-memory control state, a Solver executes them, and a Validator decides which trajectories enter memory while feeding back to guide future proposals, controlling feasibility, redundancy and coverage.
evidence: On AppWorld, BFCL v3 and MCP-Universe, Preping substantially improves over a no-memory baseline and is competitive with strong playbook-based methods built from offline or online experience, with deployment cost 2.99x lower on AppWorld and 2.23x lower on BFCL v3 than online memory construction; analyses show gains come from proposer-side control and selective updates rather than synthetic volume alone.
not_tested: The abstract does not state whether the pre-built memory is consumed via a retriever or as a static playbook at deployment, so the retrieval component's contribution is not isolated; it also does not report how the gain scales with synthetic bank size or how noisy the gains are across runs.
axes: compiled and static alternatives to retrieval
environment properties that make retrieval necessary
title: PREPING: Building Agent Memory without Tasks

claim: Multi-hop evidence retrieval planning, not answer generation, is the primary bottleneck for agentic long-video QA, with frontier agents scoring below 50% under enforced retrieval necessity but near-perfect with gold evidence clips.
method: LongVidSearch, a benchmark of 3,000 questions over 447 long videos (average 26 minutes) where a Hop-k question requires exactly k necessary clips, with a unified tool interface that fixes the retrieval backend and isolates query formulation and iterative retrieval planning, measuring accuracy and tool-call cost, evaluating VideoAgent-style agents with multiple backbone LLMs via three-judge majority voting.
evidence: Four reasoning categories with 2-, 3- and 4-hop requirements; GPT-5 reaches 42.43 accuracy versus Gemini 3 Pro 30.97 and GPT-4o 19.20; performance becomes near-perfect with gold evidence clips.
not_tested: Only one agent design (VideoAgent-style) is varied over backbones, so whether different retrieval-planning strategies close the gap is untested; the fixed retrieval backend means retriever quality itself is not varied, and run-to-run variance of the accuracy numbers is not reported.
title: LongVidSearch: An Agentic Benchmark for Multi-hop Evidence Retrieval Planning in Long Videos

claim: Agents adopt conflicting retrieved memory at the first exposed decision point even when it is task-wrong, repeated exposure amplifies the error and recovery is weak, so once agents comply their success collapses to a low floor and stronger agents suffer larger absolute damage.
method: Proposes Entry-Propagation-Recovery (E-P-R), a trajectory-level diagnostic framework asking where memory first changes an action, whether the change carries forward, and whether the agent recovers after divergence, instantiated on WebArena and on a purpose-built controlled benchmark, MemTrapBench.
evidence: WebArena and MemTrapBench across multiple unnamed models; conflicting memory induces similar compliance rates across models, and after compliance success rates collapse to a low floor; no numeric headline figures are given in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether correct or non-conflicting memory yields the symmetric benefit (how much retrieved memory helps when it is right), and whether compiled/static instructions or random exemplars induce the same compliance behavior as retrieved entries.
title: The Compliance Trap: Diagnosing How AI Agents Consume Conflicting Memory

claim: Machine learning systems generalize poorly in part because they lack latent learning (acquiring task-irrelevant information for future use), and episodic memory via retrieval can complement parametric learning to enable more flexible reuse of experiences.
method: Argues from cognitive science, links failures such as the reversal curse and agent-based navigation to missing latent learning, and shows that a system with an oracle retrieval mechanism generalizes better across these challenges, identifying within-example in-context learning as essential for using information across retrieved examples.
evidence: Language-modeling (reversal curse) and agent-based navigation settings with an oracle retrieval mechanism; models and numeric results are not stated in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether a realistic, non-oracle retriever recovers the gains, and whether the same experiences compiled once into parameters or a static prompt would match query-time retrieval.
axes: compiled and static alternatives to retrieval
title:
Latent learning: episodic memory complements parametric learning by
  enabling flexible reuse of experiences

claim: RL-based agentic search overcomes the single-turn, heuristic limits of traditional RAG by letting LLMs plan, retrieve and reflect adaptively, and the field can be organized by what RL is for, how RL is used, and where it is applied.
method: A survey organizing RL-based agentic search methods along three dimensions (functional roles, optimization strategies, scope of optimization) and summarizing representative methods, evaluation protocols, applications and open challenges, with an accompanying paper repository.
evidence: Survey only; no experiments, models or headline numbers are reported.
not_tested: No empirical comparison of surveyed methods under a common protocol, and no measurement of whether learned retrieval control beats fixed retrieval schedules or no retrieval at all.
title: A Comprehensive Survey on Reinforcement Learning-based Agentic Search: Foundations, Roles, Optimizations, Evaluations, and Applications

claim: In realistic RAG pipelines the effect of LLM positional bias is marginal because state-of-the-art retrievers place highly distracting passages at the top ranks alongside relevant ones, so rearranging passages by positional preference performs no better than random shuffling.
method: Extensive experiments on three benchmarks measuring how positional bias affects use of relevant passages and susceptibility to distracting passages under state-of-the-art retrieval pipelines, comparing position-aware rearrangement strategies against random shuffling.
evidence: Three unnamed benchmarks with state-of-the-art retrieval pipelines; over 60% of queries contain at least one highly distracting passage in the top-10 retrieved; position-aware rearrangement does not outperform random shuffling.
not_tested: Agentic or multi-step settings where retrieved items are trajectories or exemplars rather than passages, and whether the conclusion holds with far more than 10 passages in very long contexts.
title: Do RAG Systems Suffer From Positional Bias?

claim: Current memory agents fall short of mastering all four core memory competencies (accurate retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding, conflict resolution), and existing benchmarks do not evaluate them in an incremental multi-turn setting.
method: Introduces MemoryAgentBench, combining reformulated existing datasets and newly constructed ones covering the four competencies under incremental multi-turn interaction, and evaluates memory agents ranging from simple context-based and RAG systems to agents with external memory modules and tool integration.
evidence: MemoryAgentBench; a diverse set of memory agents (context-based, RAG, external memory modules, tool integration); the headline finding is that no current method masters all four competencies, with no numeric figures in the abstract.
not_tested: Token cost or latency accounting of long-context versus retrieval agents, and run-to-run variance of the reported agent results.
title: Evaluating Memory in LLM Agents via Incremental Multi-Turn Interactions

claim: Structured multimodal tutorials distilled from human screen recordings and interaction logs are effective knowledge representations that improve both human learning and GUI-agent planning and generalization, surpassing human-authored tutorials.
method: A pipeline that records human experience, parses it with a multimodal Action Parser into perception, action and intent, abstracts steps into hierarchical task graphs with a Step Planner, and composes reusable image-text instructions with a Tutorial Composer, evaluated on a new benchmark derived from official software documentation and in downstream GUI-agent planning.
evidence: A new tutorial-generation benchmark from official software documentation; tutorials reported to surpass human-authored ones and significantly outperform baseline methods, with faster human task completion and improved GUI-agent planning; no numeric figures in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether tutorials are supplied statically or retrieved per task, how the gain compares to giving the agent raw or retrieved demonstrations, and how well tutorials generalize across applications beyond the documented software.
axes: compiled and static alternatives to retrieval
title: Demo2Tutorial: From Human Experience to Multimodal Software Tutorials

claim: Both exact and overly approximate retrieval degrade search-agent efficiency, and scheduling and retrieval stalls cause cascading latency; high-recall approximate retrieval with priority-aware scheduling and non-stall retrieval removes these bottlenecks without hurting generation quality.
method: Introduces SearchAgent-X, an inference framework for LLM-based search agents that combines high-recall approximate retrieval with priority-aware scheduling and non-stall retrieval, compared against vLLM and HNSW-based retrieval systems.
evidence: Diverse tasks against vLLM and HNSW-based retrieval baselines; up to 3.4x higher throughput and 5x lower latency with no loss of generation quality.
not_tested: Token or cost accounting of the retrieved content itself rather than latency and throughput, and whether the efficiency gains hold for agent memory retrieval over trajectories rather than document search.
title:
Demystifying and Enhancing the Efficiency of Large Language Model Based
  Search Agents

claim: Many long-context LLMs can follow multiple information threads simultaneously without significant loss, but for many models the effective context limit is substantially shorter than the supported length with accuracy declining as the context grows, and token counts from different tokenizers are not directly comparable.
method: A set of retrieval experiments on 17 leading LLMs measuring the ability to follow single and multiple threads of information through near-million-token haystacks composed mostly of irrelevant content.
evidence: 17 leading LLMs on near-million-scale haystacks; many models are described as threadsafe; effective context is often significantly shorter than supported context; no specific numbers in the abstract; code and data released.
not_tested: Whether a retriever over the same haystack matches or beats in-context reading at lower cost, and whether findings on synthetic threads transfer to agent memory banks of trajectories.
title:
Needle Threading: Can LLMs Follow Threads through Near-Million-Scale
  Haystacks?

claim: Refining retrieved content through meta-prompting optimization before it enters the prompt improves retrieval-augmented generation by over 30% on multi-hop question answering.
method: A meta-prompting optimization step that refines retrieved content (addressing excessive volume, dispersion and out-of-focus material) before inclusion in the prompt, compared against an otherwise similar RAG system without the refinement.
evidence: StrategyQA multi-hop QA; over 30% improvement versus a similar retrieval-augmented system without the method; models are not stated in the abstract.
not_tested: Only one dataset is used; the token cost of the extra meta-prompting call is not accounted for; no comparison against simply retrieving fewer passages or random passages.
title: Meta-prompting Optimized Retrieval-augmented Generation

claim: LLMs and VLMs can abstract sub-optimal demonstrations plus human feedback into a memory of insight-annotated exemplars that, when used as prompt examples in retrieval-augmented agents, substantially improve decision-making and reduce reliance on expert-crafted examples.
method: In-Context Abstraction Learning (ICAL): a VLM abstracts a noisy demonstration into a general program by fixing inefficient actions and annotating task relationships, object state changes, temporal subgoals and task construals, refines these interactively with human feedback during execution, and stores them as exemplars for a retrieval-augmented agent; fine-tuning on them is also tested.
evidence: TEACh (+12.6% goal-condition success), VisualWebArena (task success 14.3% to 22.7% over SOTA), Ego4D action forecasting (beats few-shot GPT-4V, competitive with supervised models); outperforms in-context learning from action plans lacking insights; fine-tuning yields further gains.
not_tested: Whether the abstracted insights work as a fixed exemplar set without a retriever, how gains vary with memory size or number of exemplars, and retrieval versus random exemplars is not reported in the abstract.
axes: compiled and static alternatives to retrieval
title:
ICAL: Continual Learning of Multimodal Agents by Transforming
  Trajectories into Actionable Insights
